pages.text: After dinner, Dingding pushed the bowl aside and crawled under the blanket. The night lamp glowed. "I don't want to brush. I'm sleepy!"
Mom, who worked several paddies on her own, held out a toothbrush. Dingding refused and went to sleep.
That night, something tickled between Dingding's teeth. Dingding poked with their tongue and pressed their cheek. Their eyes opened wide.
Grandma, who had farmed rice all her life, brought a lantern. She looked inside Dingding's mouth. A grain of rice was stuck between the teeth.
Grandma gently removed the grain and showed it on her palm. "If it stays there all night, your teeth may ache. What should we do?"
"A toothbrush is a tiny broom. Sweep your teeth just as we sweep the bank. Say goodbye to the rice!" Grandma sang, "Brush, Brush—Bye, Rice!" Dingding sat up.
Grandma held the basin. Dingding put toothpaste on the brush and brushed up and down. White bubbles appeared. "Brush, Brush—Bye, Rice!"
Dingding rinsed and opened their mouth. Nothing was left between the teeth. They felt smooth, and Dingding's breath smelled fresh.
They made a plan: brush when the ducks called in the morning, and brush after dinner. Sweep up and down, like sweeping the bank. The next day, Dingding reached for the brush at the first duck call.
Mom hugged Dingding. "Your teeth are as neat as rows of corn kernels!" Dingding brushed before bed, with no aching teeth, and waved the brush toward the doorway. "Brush, Brush—Bye, Rice!"
